people.bio: Alan Turing was a British mathematician, logician, and computer scientist whose 1936 paper on computable numbers laid the formal foundations of modern computing, and whose wartime cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park broke the German Naval Enigma and shortened the Second World War. After the war he pioneered theoretical computer science at Manchester and proposed the imitation game that bears his name as a benchmark for machine intelligence. In 1952, after a burglary investigation surfaced his relationship with a man, he was prosecuted for "gross indecency" and accepted chemical castration with diethylstilbestrol to avoid prison; he died in 1954 in circumstances ruled at the time to be suicide by cyanide. The British government issued a formal apology in 2009 and a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.
people.quote: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.

people.bio: Albert Cashier was an Irish-born American who enlisted in the 95th Illinois Infantry of the Union Army in 1862 and fought in roughly forty engagements during the United States Civil War, including the Siege of Vicksburg and the Red River Campaign. After the war he settled in Saunemin, Illinois, where he worked as a farmhand and handyman, voted, and drew a veteran's pension under his name for the rest of his working life. His assigned sex at birth was disclosed only late in life after a road accident, and the army subsequently confirmed his service record and pension under his lived name. He is the longest-documented case of a person assigned female at birth serving openly as a male soldier and living the rest of his life as a man in nineteenth-century America.

Albert McLeod is a Métis and Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation activist from Manitoba who has worked since the 1980s on Indigenous HIV/AIDS response, Two-Spirit organising, and LGBTQ+ rights in Canada. He was a participant at the 1990 gathering in Beausejour, Manitoba where the English term 'Two-Spirit' was adopted in place of colonial categories, and is a co-founder of the Two-Spirited People of Manitoba and a public educator on Indigenous queer history.

Audre Lorde was a Black lesbian poet, essayist, and theorist of difference whose work — from Coal and The Black Unicorn to Sister Outsider and The Cancer Journals — refused the demand that she choose between her race, sexuality, and politics. She helped found Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press in 1980, taught at Hunter College and elsewhere, and built durable solidarities between Black, Caribbean, and Afro-German feminists; her sustained correspondence with women in Berlin in the 1980s helped catalyse the Afro-German movement. She died of breast cancer in 1992 on St. Croix, where she had taken the African name Gamba Adisa, "Warrior: She Who Makes Her Meaning Known."
people.quote: Your silence will not protect you.

people.bio: Barbara May Cameron was a Hunkpapa Lakota writer, photographer, poet, and activist from Standing Rock who co-founded Gay American Indians in San Francisco in 1975 alongside Randy Burns, creating the first organisation in the United States by and for LGBTQ+ Native people. She worked through the Lesbian Agenda for Action, the San Francisco Human Rights Commission, and the United Nations on Indigenous, women's, and LGBTQ+ rights, and was a vocal advocate for HIV/AIDS services in Native communities during the height of the epidemic.

Bayard Rustin was an African American civil rights strategist, pacifist, and labour organiser who introduced Gandhian non-violent direct action to the United States civil rights movement and served as the chief organiser of the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. An openly gay man at a time when that was both criminal and politically weaponised, he was repeatedly pushed into the background of movements he had built — including by allies who feared his sexuality and his earlier Communist affiliations would be used to discredit them. He continued organising for labour, refugee, and LGBTQ causes through the rest of his life, and was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

Beverley Palesa Ditsie is a South African film-maker and activist who co-founded the Gay and Lesbian Organisation of the Witwatersrand alongside Simon Nkoli in the late 1980s and helped organise the first Pride march on the African continent in Johannesburg in 1990. At the 1995 United Nations Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing she became the first openly lesbian woman to address the UN on lesbian rights as human rights. Her documentary films, including Simon and I and Lesbians Free Everyone, continue the archival and advocacy work she began in her teens.

The Chevalière d'Éon was a French diplomat, soldier, and spy who served Louis XV's secret diplomacy in Russia and Britain in the mid-eighteenth century, and who lived the second half of her life — from 1777 until her death in 1810 — publicly as a woman with official French recognition. Bets on her assigned sex were openly traded on the London Stock Exchange in the 1770s. Postmortem examination found her anatomy to be male; she had insisted throughout her later life on living and being addressed as a woman. Her case fascinated her contemporaries and lent her name to the now largely abandoned medical term "eonism" for what would later be discussed as transgender experience.

Emperor Ai was the penultimate ruler of the Western Han dynasty, reigning over China from 7 BCE until his death in 1 BCE. The official Han histories record his devoted relationship with the courtier Dong Xian, including the often-told story that the emperor cut off his own sleeve rather than wake his sleeping lover — the source of the Classical Chinese euphemism duànxiù ("the passion of the cut sleeve") for male same-sex love. Several earlier Han emperors had documented male favourites as well, and the court annals discuss these relationships matter-of-factly rather than as scandal. His reign is a standing rebuttal to the claim that same-sex love is a modern Western invention.

Frank Kameny was an American astronomer whose 1957 dismissal from the United States Army Map Service for being gay launched a six-decade campaign against federal anti-gay employment policy. He filed the first known civil-rights claim based on sexual orientation in the United States Supreme Court in 1961, co-founded the Mattachine Society of Washington, and led picket lines outside the White House and Independence Hall years before the Stonewall uprising. He coined the slogan "Gay is good," pushed the American Psychiatric Association to remove homosexuality from the DSM in 1973, and lived to see the federal government formally apologise for his firing in 2009.

Frank Mugisha is a Ugandan LGBTI rights activist who has served as executive director of Sexual Minorities Uganda since 2007, leading the coalition that for two decades has organised against successive iterations of the country's criminalising legislation, including the 2014 Anti-Homosexuality Act and the further-reaching 2023 law. He continued that work through the 2011 murder of his friend and colleague David Kato and through Uganda's 2022 order shutting SMUG down. He has received the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Award and the Rafto Prize for human-rights work conducted at sustained personal risk.

Harvey Milk was an American politician who in 1977 became one of the first openly gay candidates elected to public office in the United States, taking a seat on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors after three earlier campaigns. He sponsored the city's gay civil-rights ordinance, organised the 1978 statewide defeat of the Briggs Initiative which had sought to bar gay teachers from California's public schools, and built coalitions with labour, Chinese American merchants, and seniors in the Castro and beyond. He was assassinated in City Hall in November 1978, alongside Mayor George Moscone, by former supervisor Dan White. He was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009.

Ifti Nasim was a Pakistani American poet who left Lahore for the United States in 1971 and built a long writing life in Chicago that included Narman in 1994, the first published collection of openly gay-themed poetry in Urdu. He co-founded Sangat in 1986, one of the earliest support and social networks for queer South Asians in North America, and hosted a long-running Urdu-language radio programme in Chicago alongside a day job in luxury car sales. He continued reading, writing, and mentoring younger South Asian queer writers until his death in 2011.

James Baldwin was an African American novelist, essayist, and civil-rights commentator whose books — among them Go Tell It on the Mountain, Giovanni's Room, Another Country, and The Fire Next Time — examined race, sexuality, and the moral interior of the United States with a precision few of his contemporaries matched. Living much of his adult life in France, he wrote openly about love and desire between men at a time when American publishers warned this would end his career, and he refused to subordinate either his race or his sexuality to the other in his political analysis. He continued lecturing, debating, and writing on race, empire, and queer life until his death in Saint-Paul-de-Vence in 1987.

Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir is an Icelandic politician who served as Prime Minister of Iceland from 2009 to 2013, taking office during the country's banking collapse and becoming the first openly LGBTQ+ head of government in the modern world. Earlier in her career she served as Minister of Social Affairs and held a parliamentary seat for more than thirty years, focusing on housing, social welfare, and gender equality. She entered a civil union with the author Jónína Leósdóttir in 2002 and their union was converted to a marriage on 27 June 2010, the day Iceland's gender-neutral marriage law took effect.

Kasha Jacqueline Nabagesera is a Ugandan LGBTI rights activist who founded Freedom and Roam Uganda in 2003 and later launched Bombastic Magazine to publish first-person stories by Ugandan LGBTI people in a hostile media environment. She was a lead plaintiff in the 2010 case that won an injunction against the tabloid Rolling Stone after it published lists of alleged gay Ugandans under the headline "Hang Them". She has received the Martin Ennals Award and the Right Livelihood Award for human-rights work carried out under sustained legal and physical threat, and continues organising from Uganda and in exile.

Khalid Abdel-Hadi is a Jordanian editor and designer who in 2007, at seventeen, founded My.Kali Magazine — an Arabic and English online publication for LGBTQ+ voices from the SWANA region — after appearing on its first cover. The magazine has published cultural criticism, journalism, and creative writing from across the Arabic-speaking world in the face of recurring government bans, online blocking, and online harassment campaigns. He has continued as editor-in-chief of My.Kali while building a parallel career in graphic design and curation, and remains one of the most visible openly gay Arab editors working in the region today.

Leo Varadkar is an Irish Fine Gael politician and qualified general practitioner who served as Taoiseach from 2017 to 2020 and again from 2022 to 2024 — the first openly gay person and the first person of partial Indian descent to hold the office. He came out publicly during the campaign for the 2015 referendum that introduced civil marriage equality to the Irish Constitution by popular vote. Before and after his terms as head of government he held senior ministerial roles in transport, health, social protection, and enterprise.

Lili Elbe was a Danish painter who in 1930 and 1931 underwent a series of gender-affirming surgeries in Berlin and Dresden, supervised by Magnus Hirschfeld's Institut für Sexualwissenschaft and surgeon Kurt Warnekros. She is among the earliest documented recipients of such surgery in modern Europe, and Denmark formally annulled her prior marriage and recognised her under her chosen name. She died in 1931 of complications following a uterine transplant attempt — an experimental procedure far beyond the medical capacities of her time. Her partially fictionalised memoir was published posthumously in 1933 and has shaped public understanding of her life ever since.

Magnus Hirschfeld was a German Jewish physician and sexologist who founded the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee in 1897 — the first sustained organisation campaigning for the decriminalisation of homosexuality — and the Institut für Sexualwissenschaft in Berlin in 1919, which combined clinical care, archive, and advocacy. His clinic developed some of the earliest protocols for gender-affirming surgery and identification papers for trans patients including Dora Richter and Lili Elbe. The Nazis identified him as a triple target — gay, Jewish, and socialist — and student paramilitaries looted and burned the Institut's library in May 1933 while Hirschfeld was abroad. He died in exile in Nice two years later.

Manvendra Singh Gohil is the crown prince of the princely house of Rajpipla in Gujarat, India, and the first member of a former Indian royal family to publicly come out as gay, in a Gujarati newspaper interview in 2006. The disclosure prompted threats of disinheritance and effigy-burnings in Rajpipla, but he continued the work that prompted it: founding the Lakshya Trust in 2000 to deliver HIV prevention, sexual-health education, and community support across Gujarat. He campaigned alongside other Indian activists for the Supreme Court decision in 2018 that read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, decriminalising consensual same-sex relations between adults.

Marsha P. Johnson was a Black American drag performer, sex worker, and street activist who was a central figure in New York's queer scene around the 1969 Stonewall uprising and the gay liberation movements that followed. With Sylvia Rivera she co-founded Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries (STAR) in 1970, providing food, clothing, and shelter to homeless trans youth and street queens; she also performed with the drag troupe Hot Peaches and modelled for Andy Warhol. She survived years of poverty, police violence, and incarceration before her body was found in the Hudson River in 1992; the New York Police Department reclassified her case as undetermined in 2012 amid renewed community pressure.

Nergis Mavalvala is a Pakistani American astrophysicist and the Curtis and Kathleen Marble Professor of Astrophysics at MIT, where she became Dean of the School of Science in 2020. Her experimental work on quantum optical measurement and laser interferometry was foundational to the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory's 2015 direct detection of gravitational waves from a binary black hole merger, a result recognised with the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for the LIGO leadership. Openly queer and an out member of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, she has spoken about visibility for LGBTQ scientists, particularly within Pakistani and South Asian communities, alongside her continued research on quantum measurement.

Pedro Lemebel was a Chilean essayist, chronicler, novelist, and performance artist whose work made marginal Santiago — travestis, sex workers, the AIDS-era poor — its centre and named the dictatorship and its long aftermath without apology. With Francisco Casas he formed the collective Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis in 1987, staging public interventions against the Pinochet regime, and from the 1990s he produced the crónicas and the novel Tengo miedo torero that remade Chilean prose. He worked in radio, performance, and visual art alongside his writing, and continued publishing until his death from laryngeal cancer in 2015.

Roberta Cowell was a British racing driver and Second World War Spitfire pilot who, in 1951, became the first known British trans woman to undergo gender-affirming surgery, following hormonal treatment and a vaginoplasty performed by surgeon Sir Harold Gillies. She had been shot down over Germany and survived a prisoner-of-war camp; after the war she returned to motor racing and competed at Shelsley Walsh and elsewhere under her own name. Her 1954 autobiography was a public sensation in the British press of the day. She lived the rest of her long life in relative privacy and died in 2011.

Sally Ride was an American physicist and NASA astronaut who in June 1983 became the first American woman in space aboard STS-7, returning a year later for STS-41-G. After leaving NASA she served on the Rogers Commission investigating the Challenger disaster and later on the Columbia Accident Investigation Board, and she founded Sally Ride Science to broaden girls' access to science and engineering education. Her twenty-seven-year partnership with the writer and educator Tam O'Shaughnessy was disclosed publicly in her obituary in 2012 after her death from pancreatic cancer, making her the first acknowledged LGBTQ+ astronaut.

Sappho was an Archaic Greek lyric poet of the seventh-to-sixth century BCE who lived on the island of Lesbos and composed monodic verse for performance with the lyre, including ardent love poems addressed to women and girls within her circle. Only one of her poems survives complete; the rest reach us as fragments quoted by later grammarians or recovered from papyrus scraps in the Egyptian sands. The Library of Alexandria collected her work in nine books, and Plato called her the tenth Muse. Her name and her island gave the modern English words "sapphic" and "lesbian" their meaning, but her poems themselves long predate, and outlast, any modern label.

Sharice Davids is a Ho-Chunk Nation member, attorney, and former mixed martial artist who in 2018 became one of the first two Native American women elected to the United States Congress, and the first openly LGBTQ+ Native American in Congress. Representing Kansas's 3rd district, she has worked on tribal sovereignty, infrastructure, small business, and reproductive rights. Before politics she was a White House Fellow under President Obama and a community organiser on the Pine Ridge Reservation.

Simon Nkoli was a South African anti-apartheid, gay-rights, and HIV/AIDS activist who came out to his fellow accused during the Delmas Treason Trial of the mid-1980s, forcing the United Democratic Front to confront its own homophobia and ultimately winning the support of his co-defendants. After his acquittal and release in 1988 he co-founded the Gay and Lesbian Organisation of the Witwatersrand and organised the first Pride march on the African continent in Johannesburg in October 1990. His lobbying contributed to the inclusion of the world's first constitutional protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in South Africa's 1996 Constitution. He died of AIDS-related illness in 1998.

Sylvia Rivera was a Latina American street activist of Puerto Rican and Venezuelan descent who, alongside Marsha P. Johnson, co-founded Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries in 1970 to feed and house homeless trans and gender-nonconforming youth in lower Manhattan. She had been part of the crowd resisting the police raid on the Stonewall Inn in 1969 and spent the next three decades pushing the gay-rights movement to keep trans people, sex workers, and the homeless in its frame — most famously in her 1973 "Y'all Better Quiet Down" speech at New York's Christopher Street Liberation Day rally. She continued organising through poverty, addiction, and recovery, dying in 2002 shortly after founding Transy House and reviving STAR.

Tammy Baldwin is an American attorney and politician from Wisconsin who in 1998 became the first openly LGBTQ+ non-incumbent elected to the United States House of Representatives, and in 2012 the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to the United States Senate. Her legislative work has centred on healthcare access, manufacturing policy, and dairy-state economic issues alongside LGBTQ rights, including co-sponsorship of the Respect for Marriage Act enacted in 2022. She has been re-elected to the Senate twice and continues to serve representing Wisconsin.

Vladimir Luxuria is an Italian actress, writer, and politician who in 2006 was elected to the Italian Chamber of Deputies for the Communist Refoundation Party, becoming the first openly transgender member of any European parliament. Earlier she had organised Rome's Muccassassina nightclub nights and the city's Pride marches in the 1990s. Since leaving parliament in 2008 she has continued in television, theatre, and activism, including high-profile interventions on LGBTQ rights at the 2014 Sochi Olympics where she was briefly detained for displaying a rainbow flag.

We'wha was a Zuni Lhamana, a person assigned male at birth who took on traditional women's social and ceremonial roles within Zuni society in present-day New Mexico. A renowned weaver and potter, We'wha became a cultural ambassador and from late 1885 to mid-1886 travelled to Washington, D.C. for six months at the invitation of anthropologist Matilda Coxe Stevenson, meeting President Grover Cleveland and members of Congress, who understood her as a Zuni woman. Her life is one of the most extensively documented pre-twentieth-century records of an Indigenous gender-diverse public figure and is often cited as foundational in Two-Spirit history.

Xavier Bettel is a Luxembourgish politician of the Democratic Party who served as Prime Minister of Luxembourg from 2013 to 2023 and since 2023 has served as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs. In 2015 he married the Belgian architect Gauthier Destenay, becoming the first sitting European Union head of government to enter a same-sex marriage. His tenure as Prime Minister coincided with Luxembourg's legalisation of same-sex marriage in 2014 and a series of further LGBTQ-rights and bioethical reforms.

groups.name: AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power
groups.about: Direct-action group founded in New York City in 1987 to confront government and pharmaceutical inaction during the HIV/AIDS crisis, whose protests reshaped drug approval, treatment access, and public discourse about the epidemic in the United States and abroad.

groups.name: [Test] Ancient and Pre-Modern Queer Voices
groups.about: Fixture grouping for documented pre-modern figures whose lives, poetry, or court records describe same-sex love and gender variance long before modern Western identity categories.

groups.name: [Test] Early Modern Gender Crossing
groups.about: Fixture grouping for early-modern figures who lived publicly across gender lines — soldiers, diplomats, sailors, and adventurers documented in court, military, and church records.

groups.name: [Test] Early Sexology and Gender Pioneers
groups.about: Fixture grouping for researchers, clinicians, and patients of the first wave of sexological and gender-affirming medicine in late-nineteenth and early-twentieth century Europe.

groups.name: Gay and Lesbian Memory in Action
groups.about: South African archive and advocacy organisation based at the University of the Witwatersrand, dedicated to collecting and preserving the histories of LGBTQ life and organising across southern Africa.

groups.name: Gay American Indians
groups.about: Founded in San Francisco in 1975 by Randy Burns (Northern Paiute) and Barbara May Cameron (Hunkpapa Lakota), Gay American Indians is the first organisation in the United States created by and for LGBTQ+ Native Americans. The group has been central in recovering Indigenous queer and gender-diverse histories and in advocating for Two-Spirit visibility in both Indigenous and LGBTQ+ movements.

groups.name: Gay Liberation Front
groups.about: Radical gay liberation organisation founded in New York City in the weeks after the 1969 Stonewall uprising, modelled on broader liberation politics and quickly inspiring sister groups in London, Sydney, Paris, and beyond.

groups.name: Gay and Lesbian Organisation of the Witwatersrand
groups.about: South African gay and lesbian organisation founded in Johannesburg in 1988, notable as one of the first non-racial LGBTQ groups under apartheid and the organiser of the first Pride march in Africa in 1990.

groups.name: Institut für Sexualwissenschaft
groups.about: Pioneering Berlin research institute founded by Magnus Hirschfeld in 1919, which combined clinical care, archive, library, and advocacy on sexual and gender variance until Nazi-led students looted and burned its holdings in May 1933.

groups.name: Lakshya Trust
groups.about: Gujarat-based community trust founded by Manvendra Singh Gohil to deliver HIV prevention, sexual-health education, and community support for men who have sex with men and transgender people across western India.

groups.name: Mattachine Society
groups.about: One of the earliest sustained gay-rights organisations in the United States, founded in Los Angeles in 1950 by Harry Hay and others, which built local chapters across the country and produced foundational mid-century homophile publications and legal challenges.

groups.name: My.Kali Magazine
groups.about: Arabic and English LGBTQ+ online magazine founded in Amman, Jordan in 2007, publishing journalism, cultural criticism, and queer Arab voices across the SWANA region under sustained political and legal pressure.

groups.name: [Test] Queer Letters and Public Thought
groups.about: Fixture grouping for novelists, essayists, poets, and public intellectuals whose openly queer lives shaped twentieth- and twenty-first-century literature and political thought.

groups.name: [Test] Openly LGBTQ Political Firsts
groups.about: Fixture grouping for openly LGBTQ+ politicians who held office as the first of their kind at the national level — heads of government, ministers, senators, and parliamentarians.

groups.name: [Test] Openly LGBTQ Scientists and Engineers
groups.about: Fixture grouping for scientists, mathematicians, and engineers whose openly LGBTQ+ identity is part of the public record alongside their technical contributions.

groups.name: Sangat Chicago
groups.about: South Asian LGBTQ community organisation co-founded by Ifti Nasim in Chicago in 1986, one of the earliest support and social networks for queer South Asians in North America.

groups.name: Sexual Minorities Uganda
groups.about: Ugandan coalition of LGBTI organisations founded in 2004 to advocate for legal recognition, healthcare, and protection from violence under repeated waves of criminalising legislation, ordered closed by the Ugandan government in 2022.

groups.name: Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries
groups.about: Mutual-aid and political collective founded in New York City in 1970 by Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, providing housing, food, and advocacy for homeless trans youth and street queens largely abandoned by the wider gay-liberation movement of the era.

groups.name: International Two-Spirit Gathering
groups.about: Annual gathering originating at the 1990 meeting in Beausejour, Manitoba where the English term 'Two-Spirit' was adopted, drawn from the Anishinaabemowin phrase niizh manidoowag, to describe Indigenous gender-diverse and same-sex-attracted people on their own cultural terms rather than through colonial categories. The gathering rotates between communities across the United States and Canada.
